subject: Biology
description: Semi-conservative replication, helicase, polymerase, leading/lagging, telomere

questions.stem: DNA replication is described as SEMI-CONSERVATIVE because:

options.option_text: Both daughter molecules are entirely brand new
Each daughter has one old strand + one new strand
Original DNA molecule is fully preserved intact
Only half of the original strands are reused

questions.explanation: Semi-conservative replication — proven by MESELSON-STAHL experiment (1958, using ¹⁵N → ¹⁴N density shift). Each daughter DNA molecule has ONE PARENTAL strand + ONE NEWLY-SYNTHESISED strand. Watson + Crick predicted this from the double-helix structure (1953). Alternative models that were ruled out: CONSERVATIVE (parental DNA retained intact, both daughters new — Distractor 3) and DISPERSIVE (mixed segments, neither strand fully old or new).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: DNA replication starts at specific sites called:

options.option_text: Telomeres, found at the chromosome ends
Origins of replication, with specific sequences
Centromeres, at the chromosome middle areas
Promoters, near transcription start sites

questions.explanation: Origin of replication (ORI) — specific DNA sequences where replication initiates. PROKARYOTES (bacteria) — usually ONE origin per circular chromosome (E. coli's oriC). EUKARYOTES — MULTIPLE origins per linear chromosome (humans ~30,000-50,000 origins per genome) → faster replication of large genomes. Replication proceeds BIDIRECTIONALLY from each origin → replication 'bubbles' / forks form. Distractor 1 = telomeres (ends, special protective sequences). Distractor 3 = centromere (where sister chromatids attach during division). Distractor 4 = transcription, not replication.

questions.stem: The enzyme that UNWINDS the double helix during DNA replication is:

options.option_text: DNA ligase, joining DNA fragments together
Helicase, breaking H-bonds between bases
DNA polymerase, synthesising new strands
Topoisomerase, relieving downstream tension

questions.explanation: HELICASE — unwinds the double helix by breaking H-bonds between base pairs. ATP-powered. Forms the REPLICATION FORK. Other key enzymes: PRIMASE (lays RNA primer); DNA POLYMERASE (synthesises new strand 5'→3'; DNA pol III in bacteria; pol δ + ε in eukaryotes); LIGASE (joins Okazaki fragments); TOPOISOMERASE (gyrase in bacteria — relieves supercoiling tension ahead of fork); SINGLE-STRAND BINDING PROTEINS (SSB — keep separated strands apart).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: DNA polymerase synthesises new DNA in the direction:

options.option_text: 3' to 5' direction along the new strand
5' to 3' direction always on the new strand
Either direction depending on the strand
Both ends simultaneously to the middle

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase ONLY adds new nucleotides at the 3' end (i.e., synthesis goes 5' to 3'). Reading the template strand 3' to 5'. This is why replication is asymmetric: LEADING strand (template 3'→5') = synthesised continuously toward the fork. LAGGING strand (template 5'→3') = synthesised in short OKAZAKI FRAGMENTS away from fork, joined later by ligase. Why? Polymerase adds to free 3'-OH end; thermodynamics + proofreading require this directionality.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The short DNA fragments synthesised on the LAGGING strand during replication are called:

options.option_text: Telomere fragments at the chromosome ends
Okazaki fragments, joined later by ligase
Histone fragments around the DNA core
Transposon fragments inside the genome

questions.explanation: OKAZAKI FRAGMENTS — short stretches (~100-200 nucleotides in eukaryotes; ~1000-2000 in bacteria) of DNA synthesised discontinuously on the lagging strand. Each fragment starts with an RNA primer (laid by primase). After polymerase fills, primer is removed, gap filled, and DNA LIGASE joins fragments into one continuous strand. Discovered by REIJI + TSUNEKO OKAZAKI (Japan, 1968). Distractors are unrelated DNA features.

questions.stem: TELOMERES at chromosome ends shorten with each cell division. The enzyme that can extend them is:

options.option_text: DNA polymerase III, the main replicator
Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase enzyme
Restriction enzyme, cutting DNA at sites
Reverse transcriptase from HIV virus only

questions.explanation: TELOMERES — protective TTAGGG repeats at chromosome ends. Shorten ~50-200 bp per division (Hayflick limit, ~50 divisions in normal somatic cells). TELOMERASE — ribonucleoprotein with reverse-transcriptase activity, uses an RNA template to extend telomeres. Active in: stem cells, germ cells, some immune cells, and ~85% of cancers (giving cancer cells 'replicative immortality' — a hallmark of cancer). Discovered by ELIZABETH BLACKBURN, CAROL GREIDER, JACK SZOSTAK (Nobel 2009). Distractor 4 — HIV reverse transcriptase is similar in mechanism but unrelated.

questions.stem: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) uses a heat-stable DNA polymerase from:

options.option_text: E. coli, the standard lab bacterium
Thermus aquaticus, a hot-spring bacterium
Yeast, a common eukaryotic model
Human cells, providing native polymerase

questions.explanation: TAQ POLYMERASE — from Thermus aquaticus, a thermophilic bacterium discovered in Yellowstone hot springs (Brock, 1969). Optimum at 70-80°C; survives the 95°C denaturation step of PCR cycles. KARY MULLIS (Nobel 1993) invented PCR using Taq → could automate cycles without re-adding polymerase each time. PCR revolutionised molecular biology: COVID testing, forensics, paternity tests, ancient DNA work. E. coli polymerases denature at high temperatures.
